title: The Winter Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino de Invierno
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.

spans.t: The Winter Way is the quiet road out of Ponferrada. It leaves the Camino Francés where the French Way goes straight on, turns left, and follows the River Sil through Roman gold country and wine country. It climbs a hill with a view over four provinces, and comes down through the Deza to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. It is ~260 km in all, and it is a road that asks you to plan.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this quiet road is your Camino, what each of its ten walking days asks of you, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days by region, and the chapter on the long days, which shows where the official stages can be split.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your stage. If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. On a road with few pilgrims that matters more than usual. For those answers, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
Every distance here carries a tilde,

, because it is approximate. The official sources measure this road in different ways, and the book says so where it matters. Where something depends on the season (snow, fog, flooded fields, heat, a closed path), it says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say to one another as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way. Each stamp is a
sello
. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules, which the chapter on arriving sets out. The
Xunta
is the regional government of Galicia, and its official Camino portal is one of this book's main sources.
Place names follow the official pages: Spanish in the first days, in León (Las Médulas, Puente de Domingo Flórez), and Galician from the border (O Barco de Valdeorras, A Rúa, Monforte de Lemos).
Carry what you need, plan your nights ahead, and take your time over the long hill.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes

The Winter Way starts in Ponferrada, the capital of the Bierzo, a region of León. The Xunta de Galicia calls it the entrance hall to Galicia. Here the Camino Francés goes straight on, and the pilgrim on the Winter Way turns left.

The first ~43 km are in León, by the figure of the Castilla y León tourism guide: out of Ponferrada, past the Roman gold workings of Las Médulas, to Puente de Domingo Flórez at the edge of Galicia. Then the road follows the River Sil through Valdeorras, in the province of Ourense, and crosses the south of Lugo, the Ribeira Sacra. It goes on through the Deza, in Pontevedra, and ends in Santiago, in A Coruña. The Xunta says the road crosses the four Galician provinces. Ourense has only a short share of the walking: the road is longer in Lugo and in Pontevedra.

At Lalín the Xunta says the road joins the Vía de la Plata. Its stage pages put the meeting at A Laxe, ~50 km from Santiago. The last two days follow the final stretch that the Winter Way shares with the Camino Sanabrés.
How long is it?
The app's catalog gives ~260 km. The official sources do not agree, because they start counting in different places.

items.t: The Xunta's route page gives ~239 km. That is the sum of its nine stages, and they begin at Las Médulas, not Ponferrada.
The Xunta's leaflet, in Spanish, says about 260 km from Ponferrada, and its stage figures add up to ~262 km.
The Castilla y León tourism guide measures ~271 km from Ponferrada.
The Confraternity of St James says ~275 km, and so does Wikipedia.

spans.t: Plan on ~260 to ~275 km. The ten days of this book add up to ~266 km.
How many days?

The Xunta divides the road into nine stages, in both its pages and its leaflet. They are official units, not comfortable days: they run from ~14 to ~36 km, and three are longer than ~30 km. The CaminoPlus website lists the road as 10 to 12 stages. This book follows ten walking days named by the Xunta's stage towns, with Ponferrada to Las Médulas added at the start, and a chapter on the long days shows where each can be split.
Why it is called the Winter Way
The name says the road was a winter alternative. What the sources say is more careful.

The Xunta writes that "it is thought" it may have arisen as a winter alternative to the hard climb to the snowy heights of O Cebreiro, where the Camino Francés enters Galicia, and perhaps to avoid the frequent floods of the rivers of the Valcarce valley. The Confraternity of St James says it is possible that the track was preferred in winter, and that there is "as yet no firm evidence" for the theory. The Castilla y León guide is bolder: it says pilgrims used the road until the eighteenth century, and that it faded once a comfortable way opened through the Valcarce in 1788. Wikipedia says pilgrims "traditionally" used it.
So the winter story is a plausible tradition, told with different degrees of confidence. The road's Roman roots are better documented.
A short history

The Xunta says historians place the origin of the road in Roman times. A secondary Roman road is documented from the gold workings of Las Médulas towards the Via XVIII through Valdeorras, and the Roman tunnel at Montefurado is, it says, further evidence.

The stones remember pilgrims too. The Castilla y León guide says the Templar knights of the castle of Cornatel gave protection to pilgrims here, and that pilgrims had a hospital at Carucedo, beside Las Médulas. The Xunta's stage pages add the castle of Os Novaes, a Hospitaller residence, medieval hospitals at Belesar and San Pedro de Líncora, and a bridge near Rodeiro called A Ponte do Hospital, a name that recalls a pilgrims' hospital.

As a way marked and promoted for pilgrims, the road is young. The Xunta says it was made official in 2016 and calls it one of the newest Jacobean routes. The Confraternity says the Pilgrim's Office recognised it in 2015, and Wikipedia says 2016. These may be different events, and this book does not try to settle it.
What it feels like

The Xunta describes a calm that "presides" over this alternative route, which few people use, and says that calm is one of its main attractions. The Confraternity calls it a solitary road for fit and confident walkers with good basic Spanish.
The landscape does the rest. You follow the Sil, wide and deep, between slate roofs and red clay. Vineyards climb the slopes in terraces, and later come oak and chestnut woods, granaries called
hórreos
, and old bridges, some of them Roman. The walking is hilly, the days are long, and the villages are small.
What the official ratings say
The Xunta rates the Winter Way Medium-High overall. The app's catalog rates it 3 on a scale of 1 to 5, the same as the Camino Francés and one below the Camino Primitivo.

By stage, the Xunta's ratings run like this. The last day into Santiago is Low. Five stages are Medium. The stage from Quiroga to Monforte de Lemos is Medium-High. The stages from Monforte to Chantada and from Chantada to Rodeiro are High. Those two High days are consecutive.
What makes it demanding
The length of the days.

Seven of the Xunta's nine stages are between ~26 and ~36 km, and its estimates for the three longest are about seven hours of walking each. For the longest, ~36 km, that is a pace of ~5 km an hour with no stops, so plan on more.
The hills.

The road is rarely flat for long. The Xunta describes a sharp ascent to the Alto da Serra on the way to Monforte, a hard climb of about 3 km after the bridge of Belesar, and a hard ascent of ~4.8 km on Monte Faro, to over ~1,100 m. Even the last day ends with a steep climb into Santiago.
The quiet.

The Xunta says the road is little used, and the Confraternity of St James calls it solitary, with some stretches long and isolated. A Castilla y León tourism guide says services for pilgrims are not yet very abundant. The app's own note for this route says few pilgrims walk it and that you should plan accommodation ahead. A road with few walkers is a pleasure, but it means you cannot count on a stranger, a shop or a bed appearing when you need one.
The waymarking.

The Confraternity says the waymarking has improved over recent years, but that signs may still be sparse or contradictory in places, and that you should be ready to ask local people for directions. That is easier with some Spanish.
Who it suits

The Confraternity's words are the best summary: fit and confident walkers with good basic Spanish. It suits you if you have already walked several long days in a row, if you are comfortable with your own company, and if you are willing to plan each night. It suits a walker who has done the Francés and wants its opposite. It also suits anyone drawn to the Sil, the terraced vineyards, Roman remains and small stone villages more than to company on the road.
Who might choose another

If this is your first Camino and you want company, consider the Camino Francés, which the Castilla y León guide calls the best known and most used of the Jacobean routes. It has its own book in this series,
The French Way
If you have only a week, the Camino Inglés is a walk of six days, and has its own book too,
The English Way
. If mountains are what you want,
The Original Way
covers the Primitivo.
If the idea of long hours alone worries you, try a few days of it first, or choose a busier road.
Compared with its neighbours

From Ponferrada, the Camino Francés is ~209 km to Santiago, by the kilometre table of the Spanish Wikipedia. The Winter Way is ~260 km: ~50 km longer, and in return you leave the main stream of pilgrims behind.

The name promises a gentler road than the Francés, which crosses O Cebreiro at ~1,330 m. The Winter Way has its own high point on Monte Faro, and the French Wikipedia gives ~1,187 m as the highest point of the route. That is lower than O Cebreiro, but the Xunta itself offers a shorter variant around the climb of Monte Faro, which in its words avoids the snow in winter. The fair summary is that the Winter Way is the quieter road, hillier than its name suggests, with services that the Castilla y León guide calls not yet abundant.

This chapter gives patterns, not forecasts. The road crosses three kinds of country: the drier Bierzo, ringed by mountains, at the start, the deep valleys of the Sil and the Miño in the middle, and the wetter country near Santiago. The figures below come from Wikipedia's climate tables, which cite AEMET, the Spanish state weather agency, and they are averages. Any week can differ.
The short answer

The Confraternity of St James says the road is best walked between April and November. The CaminoPlus route guide says April to October. They differ by a month, and both leave out the cold months. The Confraternity adds a warning that fits the name badly: despite being called the Winter Way, the road can see the same snow, sleet, fog and high winds as the mountains of the Camino Francés, and you should expect mud, cold and wet at any time of year.
Spring: April to June

Spring is mild. In Ponferrada the average afternoon reaches ~19 °C in April, ~22 °C in May and ~27 °C in June, with nights of ~6 °C, ~9 °C and ~12 °C. In Santiago the afternoons are a little cooler, ~17 °C, ~20 °C and ~23 °C, and May still brings ~109 mm of rain. Ponferrada gets ~640 mm of rain in a year, and Santiago more than twice as much, so the end of the road is its wettest part. Carry a waterproof.
Summer: July and August

Summer is hot in the valleys. In Ponferrada the average July afternoon reaches ~30 °C, and Wikipedia says that temperatures above ~35 °C are not uncommon in heatwaves. The record is ~41.5 °C, on 17 July 2022. Wikipedia describes the Ribeira Sacra as more continental than Atlantic, with long hot summers, and the Sil valley is the more continental part. The road runs in those valleys for many days, and a long day in valley heat is the main summer hazard. In Santiago, by contrast, the average July afternoon is ~25 °C, and the month is dry, with ~31 mm of rain.
Autumn: September to November

Autumn falls inside both sources' season. September afternoons average ~26 °C in Ponferrada and ~23 °C in Santiago, and the nights are cool. Then the rain arrives: in Santiago October averages ~214 mm, the wettest month of the year, and November ~194 mm. In Ponferrada the wet months are October to December, at ~78 to ~84 mm. The Xunta warns that at the start of the stage from Monforte to Chantada, flooding is frequent in the rainy season, on completely flat stretches. Daylight shrinks: on 1 November the day lasts ~10 hours, by a standard solar calculation.
Winter: December to March

The name does not make this the easy season. In Ponferrada the average January afternoon is ~10 °C and the average night ~1 °C, nights below freezing are very common in winter, and snow falls on ~4 days a year on average. Wikipedia's record low for the town is about −10 °C.

On the road itself, the Xunta offers a shorter alternative to the climb of Monte Faro, from Penasillás, that in its words avoids the snow in winter. In Santiago the average January afternoon is ~12 °C and January brings ~196 mm of rain.

Days are short. By a standard solar calculation, daylight at Ponferrada and Santiago is ~9 hours at the December solstice, with sunrise near nine in the morning and sunset near six in the evening, Spanish time. At the June solstice it is ~15 hours, with sunset after ten at night. A winter walker has little time to waste, and a road with few services leaves little room for a late start. Places that serve pilgrims may be shut in the cold months, so ask before you rely on one.
Crowds

This is a quiet road. In February 2020 the Xunta said that more than a thousand people had walked it in the previous year. The number has probably changed since, but the shape is clear: you will meet few pilgrims, and in some seasons none. That helps with peace and hurts with company, and it is another reason to plan each night ahead.
Check before you go
Look at the forecast for the days you will walk, and ask locally about snow on Monte Faro, flooded fields near Monforte, and, in dry summers, fires and closed paths.
The credencial

The credencial is the pilgrim's passport, a folded card of stamps. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says it identifies the pilgrim, and that it has two practical uses: it gives access to the hostels of the Way, and it serves as the proof you show when you ask for the Compostela. The Office's page says it is issued by a parish church, a confraternity, a diocese, an association of friends of the Way, or another Christian institution connected with the pilgrimage. The Office's pages list confraternities and associations, in Spain and worldwide, so start there.

Stamps, the Office says, are normally collected where pilgrims sleep, but they can also be had at parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. On a road with few pilgrims, remember that list: it includes town halls. The Office's page also mentions a digital credential, an app. This book says nothing more about it, so read the Office's page before you rely on one.
Getting to Ponferrada, and home from Santiago

Wikipedia says Ponferrada lies on the A-6 motorway, has intercity bus services, and has a railway station with trains to Madrid and Barcelona. The city has no airport of its own. The nearest, León, is ~106 km to the east, and the Santiago airport is ~197 km to the north-west. Timetables change, so check them in the month you travel.

Santiago's airport is ~12 km east of the city, and the city has a railway station. Do not plan a tight connection for the day you arrive: you will want to see the Pilgrim's Office and the cathedral first.
Training

The Xunta's advice for pilgrims is to prepare physically, to plan the stages by what you can do, to pace your effort and to rest. It also says not to walk too fast in the first days, and to keep the same rhythm.

On this road that advice has teeth, because the days are long. A plan that suits a short road will not suit this one. In the weeks before you leave, practise walking ~20 km or more on two or three days in a row, with the pack you will carry, and include hills, because the road has a good many. Practise going downhill as well as up, because your knees and toes will feel the descents.
What to carry

The Xunta's leaflet gives a plain list. Wear light, loose clothes in a light colour. Carry a light waterproof that also covers your pack, a hat or other head cover, sunglasses and sun cream. Carry a sleeping bag, a small multi-tool, a torch, a mobile phone and a small first-aid kit. Its suggested kit has antiseptic, gauze, tape, plasters, a needle and thread for blisters, small scissors, petroleum jelly, mosquito repellent, antihistamines and aspirin.

Add what the Confraternity of St James says about this road: expect mud, and cold and wet weather at any time of year. A warm layer and a dry bag for it matter here. Walking poles help on the steep stretches.
Shoes and feet

The Xunta advises comfortable shoes that you have already worn, and says two pairs are a good idea. It advises well-fitting, breathable socks, clean and dry, and it says to wash your feet with soap and water at the end of the day and change your shoes. Mud is likely, so you may want boots with a good grip. Break them in before you leave.
Money and language
Carry some cash as well as a card, and do not assume that a small place will take cards: ask.

The road is walked mostly in Spanish. The Confraternity recommends good basic Spanish. From the border of Galicia the signs and place names are in Galician, which is close to Spanish, and three words help:
rúa
is a street,
ponte
a bridge and
camiño
a way. A few Spanish phrases for directions, beds and food will serve you well.
Maps, signal and booking ahead

Save an offline map before you leave home. The Confraternity says the waymarking has improved but may still be sparse or contradictory. A phone signal can fail in the valleys. The CaminoPlus app is built to work without signal. It is still in development, and what it holds for this road is described at the end of this book.

Book your nights ahead. The app's own note for this route says to plan accommodation ahead, and the Castilla y León guide says services for pilgrims are not yet very abundant. The Xunta publishes a list of hostels as a PDF on its page for the road. This book does not repeat any list, because lists change. Ask in the app, and phone or message the place the day before.

chapters.title: The Bierzo and Valdeorras: Ponferrada to A Rúa

spans.t: The character of these days

Three days take you out of León and into Galicia by the River Sil. The first is a walk from a Templar town through chestnut and slate villages to a landscape the Romans made by washing a mountain away. The second crosses the border into the province of Ourense. The third is short, along a wide river and past the caves where Valdeorras keeps its wine.

The figures come from the Xunta de Galicia. Its stage pages start at Las Médulas, so the first day uses the Xunta's leaflet and the Castilla y León tourism guide. Where these sources differ, the book says so. Treat every distance as good to a kilometre or two, and a little more on the first day.
Day 1: Ponferrada to Las Médulas (~27 km)

The Xunta's leaflet gives ~27 km for this stretch, and the Castilla y León guide adds its sections up to ~31 km. Expect between the two. The Xunta describes it as a gentle climb out of Ponferrada and a long descent to Las Médulas. Its web pages do not rate this section, so treat it as a first long day.

The Castilla y León guide has you leave from the basilica of Our Lady of La Encina, skirting the Templar castle through the old streets, to the medieval bridge over the River Boeza. The road then runs beside the Boeza and rises gently through Toral de Merayo, Villalibre de la Jurisdicción and Priaranza del Bierzo to Santalla del Bierzo. At Santalla the guide praises the view, and mentions a Templar knight carved in a tree trunk beside the way, with the inscription "Camino Real de Invierno. Vía Real de Peregrinación".

At Villavieja, the guide says, the church holds a twelfth-century image of St James as a pilgrim. The castle of Cornatel, a fortress tied to the Templars, stands on a spur above the stream, and the Xunta's leaflet says two alternatives meet on the descent from it. The climb to its foot is long and steep, so decide at the turning whether to go up. From the Alto de Ferreiros the Xunta describes a continuous descent to Las Médulas, and the Castilla y León guide has you pass through Borrenes.

Las Médulas was the most important gold mine of the Roman Empire, according to Wikipedia, and it is a World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1997. Today its red cliffs stand among chestnut trees. You are at the edge of Galicia, and the next day starts with a gentle climb.
Day 2: Las Médulas to O Barco de Valdeorras (~26 km)
The Xunta rates this stage Medium and estimates 6 hours 40 minutes. The first section follows the old royal road, the
Camino Real

, to Puente de Domingo Flórez, ~9 km, still in León. Then comes a gentle ascent to the top of Pedrices, with a fine view back over Las Médulas, and a steep descent to the last village of León, where the Xunta promises "pleasant solitude".

From Puente de Domingo Flórez you cross the Sil towards Quereño and follow the right bank to Pumares, which is already in Ourense, and on to Sobradelo. At Éntoma the Xunta singles out a Roman bridge of a single arch built of slate, and then you reach O Barco de Valdeorras.

The Xunta offers an alternative at Quereño: a detour over the Serra da Lastra, an oak wood of Mediterranean character that has been a natural park since 2002. Read this carefully. The Xunta's Spanish page says the detour is ~14 km longer. Its English page garbles the sentence into "an alternative to this 14 kilometre route", which can be read as saying the opposite. Whichever way you go, the two paths meet again at O Barco. The Xunta's table gives the main line as ~26.5 km, and the leaflet's figures imply ~26 km.
Day 3: O Barco de Valdeorras to A Rúa (~14 km)

After two long days, this is a short one: the Xunta rates it Medium, with an estimate of 3 hours 35 minutes, and its leaflet gives ~13 km. You leave O Barco by the old road, between the national road and the Sil, and cross the railway line by a flyover to Vilamartín de Valdeorras. There you cross the old bridge of A Rodeleira. The Xunta says the town has numerous caves cut into its slopes, many of them left by Roman gold-working and now turned into wine cellars, and the leaflet counts more than 400 of them. Early in August the town holds a festival of the caves, with guided visits.

From Vilamartín the road runs on long straights between the railway and the river, round the Valencia reservoir on the Sil, with a fine view of the Valdeorras valley before you enter A Rúa by the San Roque quarter. The Xunta's leaflet mentions a Roman-origin bridge in A Rúa, part of the Roman road from Braga to Astorga, and a riverside promenade.

The Valdeorras wines have a protected denomination of origin, and the leaflet names two grapes, the white godello and the red mencía. Rest here. Tomorrow is ~27 km, and the road gets hillier from here.

chapters.title: The Sil and the Ribeira Sacra: A Rúa to Chantada

spans.t: The character of these days

Three long days take you into the south of Lugo, the Ribeira Sacra. The name means "sacred riverbank", and it belongs to the canyons of the Sil and the Miño, to old monasteries and to vineyards planted on terraces called
socalcos
. In 2003 the Council of Europe included the Ribeira Sacra among its Itineraries of Interest, the Xunta says.

These are the heavy days. The stages are ~27, ~36 and ~31 km, and the Xunta rates them Medium, Medium-High and High. From here the figures are those of the Xunta's web pages. Its leaflet and the Castilla y León guide differ from them by a kilometre or three, and the chapter on long days shows where to split.
Day 4: A Rúa to Quiroga (~27 km)

The Xunta rates this stage Medium and estimates 6 hours 45 minutes. You leave A Rúa on the old road, along the line of a Roman road, and the first village, Albaredos, is already in the province of Lugo. A dirt track then drops towards the river, and soon you reach Montefurado. The Xunta calls its Roman tunnel, dug through the rock, one of the grandest Roman engineering works in the Iberian Peninsula.

After Montefurado the Sil keeps company with you, with fields of olive, fig and walnut trees. You pass A Venda Vella and A Venda Nova, where the Xunta says the ruins were once inns, and the Capela das Farrapas, a name that refers to the rags (
farrapas

) that walkers had to take off. At O Soldón the Xunta records a smithy of the Order of St John of Jerusalem. At Sequeiros you may climb to the castle of Os Novaes, a residence of the Hospitallers, and come back down. You enter Quiroga by the Rúa Real, after the medieval bridge called Ponte Pedriña.
The Xunta's table gives ~27 km. Its leaflet gives a little less, ~26.5 km, so the sources agree to within half a kilometre.
Day 5: Quiroga to Monforte de Lemos (~36 km)

This is the longest day on the road. The Xunta rates it Medium-High at ~36.5 km, with an estimate of 7 hours 20 minutes. Its leaflet says ~35 km and the Castilla y León guide ~33 km, so sources differ by up to ~3 km, and none of them makes it short.

You leave Quiroga on the right bank of the Sil and follow roads, including stretches of the provincial road, through Espandariz and Nocedo. The Xunta mentions that you may also go by San Clodio and Ribas de Sil, and cross the bridge later to rejoin the route. By the hermitage of Os Remedios you drop to the River Lor, which comes down clear from the Serra do Courel, and cross it by a medieval bridge. Then you enter the municipality of A Pobra do Brollón. On the right, the Xunta says, are the remains of the Roman gold mine of O Medo. In A Pobra itself the Xunta's photographs show the Roman bridge of A Labrada, with its Roman road.

A Pobra is ~24 km from Quiroga. After it comes a sharp ascent to the Alto da Serra and Mount Moncai. You pass Reigada and walk beside the River Seco. You enter Monforte by the Rúa Cruces, with the fortress ahead, crowned by a Benedictine monastery that the Xunta calls a thousand years old, and cross the medieval bridge over the River Cabe.

A Pobra do Brollón is the natural place to break this day: it leaves ~24 km and then ~13 km. Whether you can sleep there is a question for the app and the local sources, and this book does not answer it.

Monforte is the main town of the Terra de Lemos. The Xunta's leaflet lists its tower and walls, the monastery of San Vicente do Pino, and the college of Our Lady of the Antigua, which it says holds works by El Greco. Wikipedia says the town stands in a valley between the Miño and the Sil, and that a railway reached it in 1883. If any day deserves a rest, it is the day you arrive here.
Day 6: Monforte de Lemos to Chantada (~31 km)

The Xunta rates this stage High, estimating 7 hours 20 minutes. Its leaflet says ~31 km and the Castilla y León guide ~29 km. One warning comes first, and it comes from the Xunta's Spanish text: in the rainy season, flooding is frequent at the start of this stage, on completely flat stretches.
Check before you go.
After heavy rain, ask where you slept.

You leave Monforte by the medieval bridge and the old Rúa Abeledos, alternating stretches of road with tracks, through A Vide, A Lagoa and Pacios, to Moreda. You enter the municipality of Pantón, where the Xunta notes the manor house at O Reguengo and stones at Castrotañe that may come from a Roman road. Under old oaks you go on through O Outeiriño and A Barxa, in O Saviñao, and then Rendal and Diomondi, whose Romanesque church the Xunta singles out.

Next you go down to the bridge of Belesar over the Miño, among the terraced vineyards. At Belesar there was an ancient hospital. Then comes a hard climb of about 3 km to San Pedro de Líncora, which also had a medieval hospital, and fine views of the river. (The Xunta's English page garbles this distance; the Spanish original says about 3 km.) You enter Chantada by the district of A Ponte and the Rúa Dous de Maio.
Two splits are natural: Belesar, ~24 km in and ~6 km short of Chantada, and A Barxa, ~15 km in. A long day, a hard rating and a final climb mean that this is the day to start early.

chapters.title: Monte Faro, the Deza and the way in: Chantada to Santiago

spans.t: The character of these days

Four days take you over the last high ground and down into Santiago. The first is the climb of Monte Faro, with a view over four provinces. The next two cross the Deza, a country of oak woods, small bridges and farms, where the road meets the Vía de la Plata and shares its last ~50 km. The fourth is a short walk into the city from the south, by the Sar valley and the old gate of Mazarelos.
The figures are the Xunta's web pages again, with the leaflet and the Castilla y León guide as checks. Treat each as good to a kilometre or two.
Day 7: Chantada to Rodeiro (~26 km)

The Xunta rates this stage High and estimates 6 hours 15 minutes. Its leaflet says ~26 km and the Castilla y León guide ~27 km. You leave Chantada from the Praza de Santa Ana, climb the Rúa Uxío Novoneyra and follow a local road. Granaries (
hórreos
), roadside crosses and the
petos de ánimas
, the places where a walker leaves a small offering for the dead, as the leaflet explains, appear on the way through Centulle and San Xurxo de Asma. Ahead stands the summit of Monte Faro.

At Penasillás the road divides. The way over the mountain is, in the Xunta's words, a hard ascent of ~4.8 km, through Chao de Seixas. A turn to the left, by a way of the cross called the Camiño da Virxe, leads to the hermitage of Our Lady of O Faro, at more than ~1,100 m. The Xunta says the view takes in the four provinces of Galicia. The French Wikipedia gives ~1,187 m for the highest point of the road, on this mountain, and the Xunta's leaflet says there is a pilgrimage festival at the hermitage on 8 September.
The alternative, from Penasillás by Mouricios and San Vicente, is shorter, and the Xunta says that in winter it avoids the snow. If you see cloud on the summit, or if snow is forecast, take it.
Check before you go.

From the mountain the road goes down, past the manor of Camba, which the leaflet says once gave shelter to pilgrims, and through the valley of A Ermida, to Río and then Mouriz. In Rodeiro the town hall stands on the ruins of a fortress, and opposite it is a stone fountain with four spouts.
Day 8: Rodeiro to Bendoiro, by Lalín (~28 km)

The Xunta rates this stage Medium and estimates 6 hours 55 minutes. Its leaflet and the Castilla y León guide both say ~27 km. You follow the road towards Lalín and cross the River Arnego several times. The first bridge is A Ponte do Hospital, a name that, the Xunta says, recalls a pilgrims' hospital.

After Penerbosa you cross the medieval bridge of Pedroso. In the hamlet of A Ponte, also called Mesón, "the inn", the Xunta says that many ground floors still keep the ledges that served as counters for travellers. You climb the Coto da Mamuela, a name that refers to a field of burial mounds, and pass among chestnut trees to Palmaz.
Soon after, you enter Lalín. The town is proud of being the "zero kilometre of Galicia", the geographic centre of the land, and holds a famous fair of
cocido

, the local stew, each year. Lalín is ~22 km from Rodeiro by this book's arithmetic, with ~6 km left to A Laxe by the Castilla y León guide, and it is a natural place to stop if you want a shorter day. Beyond it, you walk by the River Pontiñas, through oak woods, beside the national road, to A Laxe, in the parish of Bendoiro. Here, the Xunta says, the Winter Way joins the Vía de la Plata.
Day 9: Bendoiro to Outeiro (~34 km)

This is the second-longest day. The Xunta rates it Medium and estimates 7 hours 5 minutes. Its leaflet says ~34 km, so the sources agree. The Xunta's last section, A Bandeira to Outeiro, is rated Medium-High.

From here to Santiago you walk the stretch shared with the Camino Sanabrés, so you may meet pilgrims who have come a long way from the south. The first metres run along the national road N-525, past Vilasoa and Prado, where a detour leads to the Marian sanctuary of O Corpiño. You cross the medieval bridge of Taboada over the River Deza, climb to Taboada and Trasfontao, and reach Silleda, ~9 km from the start.

Then a dirt road to the left of the N-525 leads to A Bandeira, ~17 km in, which splits the day almost in half. The road goes on past Santo Estevo de Oca, famous for its manor and for gardens called the "Galician Versailles". You cross the River Ulla at A Ponte Ulla, by a historic bridge, and enter the province of A Coruña, in the municipality of Vedra. Outeiro, where the Xunta's stage ends, is by the town hall of Vedra.
Day 10: Outeiro to Santiago (~17 km)

The Xunta rates this stage Low and estimates 3 hours 20 minutes. Its leaflet gives ~17 km, the same. Beyond Rubial, in the municipality of Boqueixón, a detour leads to Pico Sacro, which rises, the Xunta says, to more than five hundred metres and is linked to the legend of the translation of the Apostle's body: on its slopes grazed the wild bulls that the disciples tamed so that they would carry the body to its tomb.

You enter Compostela from the south, by the Sar district, and cross the River Sar. Then comes a last effort, the hard climb up the Rúa do Sar and the Rúa do Castrón Douro. At the top, on the right, you pass under the arch of the Porta de Mazarelos, the only gate of the old medieval wall that still stands, according to the Xunta. The last steps are by the Praza da Universidade, the Rúa da Calderería and the Praza das Praterías, to the Praza do Obradoiro. Sit down before you do anything else.

chapters.title: Long days and other ways to split

spans.t: Why this chapter exists

The Xunta's nine stages are official units, not a recommended pace, and three of them are longer than ~30 km: Quiroga to Monforte (~36 km), Monforte to Chantada (~31 km) and Bendoiro to Outeiro (~34 km). The Xunta divides each stage into sections, and the sections show where a long day can be cut.

Read the splits below as measuring points, not as promises. A point on the Xunta's list may be a village, a bridge or a hamlet, and this book does not say whether you can sleep there. Ask in the app, ask locally, and confirm the night before. For each day, the Xunta's web pages, its leaflet and the Castilla y León guide give figures that differ by a kilometre or two, and on the longest day by ~3 km. Plan for the longer figure, and carry enough water and food for it.
Where the long days can be cut
All the figures are sums of the Xunta's web sections, except where a line says otherwise, and so good to a kilometre or two.

items.t: Quiroga to Monforte (~36 km).
The sections run ~5 km to Nocedo, ~14 km to O Carballo de Lor, ~21 km to Castroncelos and ~24 km to A Pobra do Brollón. The natural cut is A Pobra: ~24 km, then ~13 km.
Monforte to Chantada (~31 km).
The sections reach Moreda at ~7 km, O Reguengo at ~10 km, A Barxa at ~15 km and Belesar at ~24 km. Cut at A Barxa for ~15 km and ~16 km, or at Belesar for ~24 km and ~6 km.
Bendoiro to Outeiro (~34 km).
Silleda is ~9 km in, which is too early to stop, and A Bandeira ~17 km in. A Bandeira splits the day into two almost equal halves.
Rodeiro to Bendoiro (~28 km).
Lalín lies ~22 km in, and then ~6 km remain to A Laxe, by the Castilla y León guide's measure.
Las Médulas to O Barco (~26 km).
Puente de Domingo Flórez is only ~9 km in, so cutting there is rarely useful.

spans.t: A twelve-day shape
Cut the two longest days and you get twelve:

items.t: Ponferrada to Las Médulas, ~27 km
Las Médulas to O Barco de Valdeorras, ~26 km
O Barco de Valdeorras to A Rúa, ~14 km
A Rúa to Quiroga, ~27 km
Quiroga to A Pobra do Brollón, ~24 km
A Pobra do Brollón to Monforte de Lemos, ~13 km
Monforte de Lemos to Chantada, ~31 km
Chantada to Rodeiro, ~26 km
Rodeiro to Bendoiro, ~28 km
Bendoiro to A Bandeira, ~17 km
A Bandeira to Outeiro, ~17 km
Outeiro to Santiago, ~17 km

spans.t: That adds up to ~267 km. The CaminoPlus website lists the road as 10 to 12 stages, and this shape is the long end of that range.
A shorter walk

If you have fewer days, the Xunta's last five stages, from Monforte to Santiago, add up to ~135 km, and its leaflet puts the same stretch at ~134 km. The last four, from Chantada, add up to ~104 km, and the leaflet gives ~103 km. Those are not figures to plan a Compostela on without asking: the chapter on arriving explains why.
Variants on the road

The Xunta names three choices, in walking order: the detour over the Serra da Lastra on Day 2, ~14 km longer than the main line; the option by San Clodio and Ribas de Sil on Day 5; and the shorter way round Monte Faro on Day 7, which in winter avoids the snow. The days are those of the ten-day plan.
Where you will sleep
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: shared rooms, bunk beds, a shared bathroom and a kitchen in some, and a
hospitalero
, the host, who stamps your credencial. The Pilgrim's Office says the credencial gives access to the hostels of the Way, so have it with you.

The Xunta runs a public network of hostels on its Camino portal, and it publishes a list of hostels as a PDF on its page for the road. The Office says that hostels with no subsidy are kept going, in austerity, by pilgrims' contributions, so leave what you can and leave the place clean. It also asks groups organised with a support car, or by bicycle, to find other shelter than the pilgrim hostels.

This book names no hostel and says where none is. Hostels open and close, and a wrong line costs a tired person dearly. On this road the point is sharper than usual. The Confraternity of St James says there are hostels, or albergues not specific to pilgrims, at various points along the way, and a Castilla y León guide says services for pilgrims are not yet very abundant. So work out your nights first, then your days. Use the app and the Xunta's list, and confirm the night before.
The Confraternity adds that there is plenty of private accommodation in the towns on the way. A road with so few pilgrims makes the evening a time to plan the next day, not just to rest.
Living with other people
Rooms are shared and the rules are simple.

items.t: Be quiet early and late.
Pack your bag the night before, and use a torch, not the ceiling light, when you leave in the dark.
Keep your boots and pack off the beds.
Some hostels ask for boots to be left at the door, so ask.
Check your bunk before you unpack.
If you find bites or bugs, tell the
hospitalero
, and if you can, wash and dry your clothes on a hot cycle.
Earplugs and a sleep mask
are the usual answer to snoring and early lights.

spans.t: Eating
A
menú del peregrino
is a set meal for pilgrims, offered in some places. This book gives no prices and names no restaurant: ask where you sleep.
Lalín holds a famous annual fair of
cocido

, the Galician stew. The Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra regions are wine country, and the wines have denominations of origin. The Castilla y León guide singles out, for the villages of the Bierzo, roasted chestnuts,
empanada
, cabbage broth, a sausage called
androlla
, country bread and almond sweets.

The practical point is the long days. The Confraternity says some stretches are long and isolated, and the Xunta's advice is to eat energetic food on the way: nuts, figs, chocolate. Buy lunch before you set out, and do not trust a village on the map to have anything open when you arrive.
Rest days

A rest day is part of a plan, not a failure of it. On this road two places suggest themselves. Monforte de Lemos comes at the end of the longest day, with its fortress, its monastery and its museums, and the Xunta's leaflet lists a good deal to see there. Santiago comes at the end, and the chapter on arriving says why to stay a second day.
If you need a rest in the middle of the road, build it into the plan, and ask in the app which of the larger places can host you.
In the evening

Wash your feet, as the Xunta advises, and look at them before you sleep. Then spend ten minutes on tomorrow: how long it is, where you will eat lunch, where the water is, and where you will sleep. On a quiet road that is the best habit you can have.

This chapter is plain on purpose. The Winter Way is a quiet road with long days and few services, and a small problem is harder to solve when no one is near. Nothing here is a reason to stay at home. It is what a careful walker does.
Feet and legs
Your feet decide how the walk goes. Stop at the first hot spot and dress it before it becomes a blister. Rest for a few minutes each hour, and eat and drink before you are hungry or thirsty.
Pace matters more than speed. The Xunta says not to walk too fast in the first days, and to keep the same rhythm. With stages of ~26 to ~36 km, the first day sets the tone for the rest.

The descents are as demanding as the climbs, and this road has long ones: from Pedrices after Las Médulas, and from Monte Faro down to the valley of A Ermida. Shorten your stride and use poles if you have them. If you feel a sharp or growing pain in a knee, a shin or the top of a foot, stop. Rest for a day, or take a shorter stage. A day lost to rest is better than a week lost to an injury.
Water

The Xunta advises drinking at least two litres a day, and never drinking from streams, rivers, springs or fountains unless you are sure the water is safe. Where villages can be far apart, leave each place with enough for the next stretch, and more on a hot day.
Heat

The valleys of the Sil and the Miño are the hot part of the road. Wikipedia describes the Ribeira Sacra as having long hot summers, says that temperatures above ~35 °C are not uncommon in Ponferrada in heatwaves, and gives ~41.5 °C as the record there, in July 2022. The Xunta advises light, loose clothes in a light colour, a head cover, sunglasses and sun cream, and avoiding the hottest hours. Start before the heat, carry more water than you think you need, and rest in the shade. If you are exhausted or have cramps, the Xunta says, rest somewhere cool and drink plenty. A headache, dizziness or nausea are signs to stop; if they do not pass, ask for help.
In dry summers, ask locally about fires and closed paths.
Check before you go.
Cold, rain and snow

The Confraternity of St James warns that the "Winter" road can have the same snow, sleet, fog and high winds as the mountains of the Camino Francés, that weather in the hills can be unpredictable, and that you should be ready for mud, cold and wet at any time of year. Wet clothes cool you fast, even in mild weather. Carry a waterproof, a warm layer, a hat and gloves, and keep one dry layer in a bag that cannot get wet. If you start to shiver, stop and get warm before you go on.
Two places call for particular care.

items.t: Monte Faro.

The climb is the highest on the road. The Xunta offers a shorter alternative from Penasillás that, in its words, avoids the snow in winter. If there is snow or cloud on the summit, take it. Look at the forecast the evening before and again in the morning.
The flat ground after Monforte.
The Xunta's Spanish text says flooding is frequent at the start of the stage to Chantada in the rainy season. After heavy rain, ask locally before you start.

spans.t: Fog, waymarking and roads

The Confraternity says the waymarking has improved but may still be sparse or contradictory in places. The Xunta's advice is never to leave the marked paths and to avoid walking when it gets dark. In fog, stay on the marked way. If you cannot see the next marker, stop, and do not guess: go back to the last one you saw. A map saved on your phone is the best backup.

Much of the road runs on tracks, and some of it runs on or beside roads. The Xunta's pages name stretches of the national road N-120 near Espandariz, the provincial road LU-933 after it, the C-533 from Rodeiro, and the national road N-525 at the start of the stage from Bendoiro, which the path then follows. Walk on the left margin of the road, facing the traffic, as the Xunta advises, and wear something bright. Never walk on a road in the dark or in thick fog.
Dogs on farms may bark as you pass. Walk on calmly, and do not stare at them or run.
Walking alone

Many people on this road walk alone for hours. Tell someone where you will sleep each night and message them when you arrive. Keep your phone charged and your map saved on it, and know the name of the last village you passed. A phone signal can fail in the valleys, so do not rely on it.
When to stop

Stop, and get help, for chest pain, a fever, severe dizziness, a fall with a blow to the head, a swollen joint, or anything that frightens you. Stop too if you are cold and cannot get warm, if you are lost in fog, or if you have run out of water. A doctor is the right person for a worry, and a plan can always change. The road will still be there.
is the European emergency number, and it works in Spain. Say where you are as exactly as you can: the village, the stage, the last landmark you passed.
Check before you go
Before each day, check the forecast, any local notice about the path, and the state of the ground: snow on Monte Faro, floods near Monforte, fires in a dry summer. Ask where you slept.
A quiet road for a quiet reason

People walk to Santiago for many reasons: faith, a promise, grief, a birthday that means something, a break from work, curiosity, sport, or no reason they could name. All of them are reasons to walk, and this book is for every one. The road asks only that you walk it honestly.
The Xunta de Galicia has a word for what this road offers. It speaks of the
sosiego
, the calm, that presides over this alternative route, which few people use, and calls that calm one of its main attractions. Whatever brings you here, you may find that the quiet is the point.
What the long days do

On a busy road, company fills the hours. On this one, the hours are yours. For some walkers that is a gift. A long day beside a river, with no one near, gives thoughts a lot of room. You may find that the first day or two are noisy inside, and that the noise settles.

For others it is hard. A road with few pilgrims can feel lonely, and an old worry may arrive on the third day with nowhere to go. If that happens, you are not doing it wrong. Walk the next hour. Stop at the next village and have something warm. Write to someone, or talk to whoever you meet. The Way has been used by people carrying heavy things for a thousand years.

If the old tradition is right, this is a road that took people around an obstacle: the snow, the floods and the high pass. Not every road is a straight line, and not every good journey is the fastest one.
Questions for the walk
Take one question a day, and let it go if it does not fit.

items.t: What are you carrying that you could put down?
What would you like to be quiet enough to hear?
Who are you walking beside, in memory or in hope?
What have you stopped noticing, and what do you notice here?
What does this day ask of you, and what can you leave to tomorrow?
If you had to say why you came, in one plain sentence, what would it be?

spans.t: For whatever you believe

The pilgrimage to Santiago is Christian in its roots, and the cathedral at its end is a place of prayer. The Pilgrim's Office has its own rules for the Compostela, and the chapter on arriving sets them out in the Office's words. Whatever you believe, be respectful in a church, and leave a village as you found it.
At the end of the day, ask yourself two things. Where did you feel most alive today? Where was it hard, and what helped? Then sleep. The next stage will keep.
The last streets

The Winter Way brings you into Santiago from the south, over the River Sar and up through the Porta de Mazarelos, and the Xunta's last steps lead through the Praza das Praterías to the Praza do Obradoiro. Wikipedia says that construction of the present cathedral began in 1075 and that it was consecrated in 1211. It is a Romanesque church with Gothic and Baroque additions, built over the reputed tomb of St James. The Baroque façade on the Obradoiro square was completed by Fernando de Casas Novoa in 1740. Behind it stands the Romanesque Pórtico da Gloria of Master Mateo, whose completion in 1188 was carved on a stone. The crypt below the high altar is, says Wikipedia, where pilgrims of the ninth-century church ended their journey.
Pilgrims' Masses are held in the cathedral, and their times change, so ask on the day. The
botafumeiro

, the great swinging censer, is used on certain important religious holidays and, Wikipedia says, at all Pilgrims' Masses in a Holy Year. 2027 is a Holy Year, and the Holy Door is opened only in Holy Years.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate that the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Office gives it to pilgrims who follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback, with the credencial stamped along the route.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

On its own pages the Office says the Certificate of Distance records the day and the starting point of your pilgrimage, the kilometres you covered, the day you arrived and the route, and that someone who has walked before can request it.
This road and the rule
From Ponferrada you have ~260 km ahead of you, far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for. A start further on is a matter of arithmetic, and the arithmetic here is uncertain.

items.t: From Chantada, the Xunta's stage lengths add up to ~104 km, and its leaflet says ~103 km. That is close to the limit, and a short detour, or a different way of measuring, changes the answer.

From Monforte de Lemos, the same stage lengths add up to ~135 km, and the leaflet says ~134 km. The Confraternity of St James gives Monforte as its suggested start for the minimum distance, at ~120 km from Santiago by its own figure. The sources differ by ~15 km.

The Xunta says the Winter Way joins the Vía de la Plata, and its stage pages put the meeting at A Laxe, ~50 km from Santiago. The Office's rule speaks of the same route. This book does not say how the Office counts a walk that begins on one route and ends on another.

spans.t: This book does not say whether any particular start counts. Ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go, say where you plan to start, and keep your credencial stamped along the way. The Office's pages on the Compostela and the credencial do not name the routes it recognises.
At the Pilgrim's Office

The Office issues the Compostela, a document in Latin. You will need your stamped credencial. Procedures and hours change, so look at the Office's own website before you arrive, and do not plan a tight connection for the same day.
Whatever the Compostela means to you, it is a record of a road you walked, not a measure of it.
The next day
Do not leave on the morning after you arrive. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it rewards a second day.

items.t: Rest.
After a road like this one, your legs have earned it.
See the cathedral without a queue behind you.
Sit in the Obradoiro square and watch the others arrive.
Think about what comes next.
If you want to keep walking, the Camino to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km, goes on from Santiago, and has its own book in this series.
Plan your way home
with the timetables in front of you, not at the last minute.

spans.t: The first days

Coming home from a quiet road can feel louder than coming home from a busy one. The streets are fast, the phone is full, and the days no longer have the shape of a walk. That is normal. Give yourself a few days before you decide what the road meant.
Keep a little of it
You do not have to keep all of it. A few small habits are enough.

items.t: Walk.
Go out for an hour a day, as you did on the road, with no purpose except the walk.
Write it down.
While the days are fresh, note three things from each stage: something you saw, something you ate, something you thought. In a year you will be glad of them.
Keep your credencial.
The stamps are a map of where you slept and who you met.
Thank someone.
A host, a stranger who gave directions, someone at home who waited for you.

spans.t: Walking again

You may want another road after this one. The Winter Way leaves the Camino Francés at Ponferrada, and the French Way has its own book in this series. The Camino Inglés and the Camino Primitivo have books too, and so do the roads to Finisterre and Muxía. This road will be here, as quiet as you left it, when you want to walk it again.
Buen Camino.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. The Camino de Invierno is on its list of routes, but this book makes no claim about what the app holds for it today, so look in the app, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.
A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. Whether it accepts anything else is for the Office to say.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Xunta de Galicia

, on its official Camino de Santiago portal (caminodesantiago.gal): the Winter Way page, in English and Spanish, with its nine stage pages and their sections, lengths, ratings and descriptions; the Xunta's leaflet on the road, a Spanish PDF; and the Xunta's press notes on the road from February 2020 and February 2022.
The Junta de Castilla y León
, on its tourism site (turismocastillayleon.com): the chapter on the Camino Real de Invierno in its guide to the traditional Caminos.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Camino Invierno, updated in June 2025.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the pages on the Compostela, the credencial, the Certificate of Distance, planning and the history of the pilgrimage.
Wikipedia

, for geography, climate tables and history: the articles on Ponferrada, Las Médulas, Monforte de Lemos, the Ribeira Sacra, Santiago de Compostela, its cathedral and airport, the Jacobean Holy Year and the Camino de Santiago route descriptions; the French Wikipedia's article on the Winter Way, for the height of Monte Faro; and the Spanish Wikipedia's article on the Camino Francés, for its kilometre table.
A standard solar calculation
, for the hours of daylight.
The CaminoPlus route catalog and route guide
, for the route's start, end, ~260 km, difficulty rating and the app's own note.

spans.t: The Xunta's English pages are machine-translated from Spanish. Two sentences read differently from the Spanish original: the length of the detour over the Serra da Lastra and the length of the climb after Belesar. Where they differ, this book follows the Spanish.

Published figures differ between these sources, so every distance in this book is marked ~. Where the sources say nothing, the book says nothing and tells you to check. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the villages and towns who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Botafumeiro
: the great censer of Santiago cathedral.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Cabildo
: the governing council of the cathedral.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hórreo
: a raised granary, a mark of the Galician countryside.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Peto de ánimas
: a wayside place where walkers leave a small offering for the dead.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
Socalcos
: terraces for vineyards on the steep slopes of the Ribeira Sacra.
Xunta
: the regional government of Galicia.
